summary: Describes and lists the functional requirements of a federated file system, and defines related terms. A federated file system lets file servers present a single namespace to clients. It is not a standards-track document; it is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Several file servers, each run by a different organisation, can present one shared tree of files to their users if the servers agree on how names map to locations. This RFC defines the words for that, and lists what such a federation must be able to do.

subtitle: How separate file servers, each run by its own organisation, can present one shared tree of files to their users.

tldr.problem: Organisations that run their own file servers want to offer clients a single namespace that spans all of them, and today the way that is assembled varies and is hard to manage.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a vocabulary of filesets, names, locations and junctions, and lists the assumptions and the fifteen requirements that a federation of file servers and namespace databases must satisfy.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document, not a protocol. It sets out what must be possible, such as creating junctions, moving and replicating filesets, and offering the shared tree over NFS or CIFS.

today: RFC 5716 is an Informational document published in January 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a requirements document rather than a protocol: it defines the terms and the behaviour that a federated file system must have, and the protocols that would carry them are left to other work.

sections.title: What a Federated File System Is
sections.content:
A federated file system is a set of file servers, run by different administrators, that present a single namespace to their clients. Today there are collections of file servers that inter-operate to provide one namespace made up of filesystem resources from different members, joined with inter-filesystem references. That namespace can be assembled at the file servers, at the clients, or by an external namespace service, and it is often not easy or uniform to manage. The requirements in this document are meant to lead to a uniform, server-based namespace that can span a whole enterprise and that is easy to manage.

The document focuses on the interfaces between the entities of the system, not on the protocols or their implementations, and does not describe the mechanisms used to implement the functionality, except where a mechanism follows inevitably from a requirement.

It defines a vocabulary. A fileset is the abstract view of a filesystem in a uniform namespace, and may be implemented behind that abstraction by one or more physical filesystems at any given time. Each fileset has a name, the FSN (fileset name), and each physical filesystem has a fileset location (FSL). A fileset is a directory tree containing files and directories, and it may also contain references to other filesets; those references are called junctions. To provide location independence, a junction does not hold information about where the real resources are, only the FSN that can be used to look up the location. The service that maps an FSN to its FSLs is the namespace database (NSDB) service. The NSDB gives a level of indirection from the virtual paths in the uniform namespace to the actual locations of files, and by design it does not store the junctions, which keeps junction administration and NSDB administration as separate roles.

The servers point clients at the right locations through existing mechanisms, such as the referrals mechanism of RFC 3530 and RFC 5661. Because the locations can be updated, migration and replication of the physical filesystems that make up the namespace can be supported in a way that is transparent to filesystem applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is that several file servers, owned by different organisations, look like one big shared filesystem to the people using them. A name in the shared tree leads to whichever server actually holds the files, wherever that is.

sections.title: What the Federation Has to Achieve
sections.content:
The stated objective is to specify a set of protocols by which file servers, or collections of file servers with different administrators, can form a federation of file servers and NSDB nodes that provides a namespace composed of the filesets hosted on them.

It should be possible for the federation to share a common namespace across all its file servers, and also possible for different file servers to project different namespaces and let clients traverse them. A federation may contain an arbitrary number of NSDB nodes, each belonging to a different administrative entity and each providing the mappings that define part of a namespace. It may also have an arbitrary number of administrative entities, each responsible for a subset of the file servers and NSDB nodes, and acting together they should be able to build and administer this multi-file-server namespace.

One thing the federation does not try to do is guarantee namespace consistency across all client views. Because different parts of the namespace may be administered by different entities, a client could be looking at a stale part of the namespace managed by one entity, because a part above it managed by another entity has changed.
sections.plainLanguage: Several organisations run their own file servers and want to offer one shared tree. Each keeps control of its own part, and the protocol has to say who owns what.

sections.title: Four Worked Examples
sections.content:
The document walks through the four basic operations with concrete steps.

Creating a fileset and its FSL. The steps are: choose the NSDB node that will keep track of the FSLs and related information for the fileset; ask that node to register a new FSN, which the node may choose itself or which the server may specify when a fileset is being restored as part of disaster recovery, so that existing junctions referencing that FSN work again; then send the FSN, the local volume path, the export path and the export options to the NSDB node, which records the information and creates the initial FSL. The process does not require any transformation of the files or the directory hierarchy. Adding a replica is then straightforward, because the NSDB node and the FSN are already known and the only remaining step is to add another FSL. The federation protocols do not include methods for creating or managing replicas, which is assumed to be a platform-dependent operation; the only requirement is that replicas be registered and unregistered with the NSDB.

Resolving a junction. When a client asks for an object that turns out to be a junction, the server resolves it to find the FSLs that implement the referenced fileset. The steps are: the server determines the object is a junction; using the junction it looks up the FSN of the target fileset locally; using the FSN it finds the NSDB node responsible for the target; it asks that node for the set of FSLs that implement the FSN and gets them back; it converts one or more of the FSLs to the location type the client uses, such as an NFSv4 fs_location; and it redirects the client to the location. Only the fourth step touches the federation protocols; the rest may use platform-specific interfaces. The RFC notes that this resolution method must work, but that it need not be the only one, and it may serve as the fallback when all else fails.

Creating a junction. Given a local path and the FSN of a remote fileset, an administrator asks the server to create a junction from the local path to the remote fileset, and the server inserts the junction to the FSN at that path into the local filesystem. Only the first step uses the federation interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives step-by-step examples: how a file tree gets a name in the shared space, how a second copy is registered, how a client is sent to the right server when it follows a link, and how an administrator creates such a link in the first place.

sections.title: The Assumptions and the Requirements
sections.content:
Several assumptions are so fundamental that the RFC treats them as basic assumptions: if any of them is violated, the rest of the requirements have to be reviewed in their entirety.

A1, the federation protocols require no changes to existing client-facing protocols, and may be extended to incorporate new ones. A2, a client should not need any prior knowledge of the general structure or composition of the federation; it may need specific knowledge to find the instance of the fileset that defines the root of its view, and discovers the rest as it traverses. A3, all requirements must be satisfiable using the federation protocols and the standard protocols the file servers use, so an operation needing an interaction between two or more members must be possible without proprietary protocols. A4, all entities taking part in a federation operation must be able to authenticate each other; the authority of a principal to ask another to do something is ultimately decided by the second, authorisation may be partitioned by server collection or by operation, and an operation attempted by an unauthorised entity must fail in a way that shows the failure was due to insufficient authorisation. A5, the federation protocols must not require changes to the existing authentication and authorisation mechanisms at the file servers for client-facing protocols. A6, an FSN must express, or be usable to discover, the location of the NSDB node responsible for the fileset's FSLs and the FSN identifier itself, because there may be many NSDB nodes and no single entity knows where they all are, so exhaustive search is not an option. A7, all federation servers and NSDB nodes are assumed to execute the protocols correctly, and behaviour is undefined in the case of Byzantine behaviour. A8, the locations of federation services must be specifiable in a way every member that accesses them can interpret.

The requirements themselves run from R1 to R15. The first four concern the FSN. Each FSN must be unique within the scope of its NSDB, so that it is globally unique; it must be descriptive enough to locate an instance of the fileset it names within the federation at any time; all FSNs must stay the same when the underlying filesystems move or are replicated, with only the mappings from FSN to FSL changing; and every file accessible from the global namespace must belong to a fileset with an assigned FSN.

R2 to R6 cover the operations. It must be possible to create an FSN for a fileset and bind an FSL to it, and these are NSDB operations requiring no action from a file server; the FSN and the FSL may exist independently of each other, which lets an administrator incorporate existing filesets into the namespace or define the namespace's shape before creating the component filesets. It must be possible to create a junction to a target fileset given its FSN, and clients must then treat the junction transparently as a reference to the FSLs that implement the FSN; it should be possible to mount one fileset at several named places; a junction created in a replicated fileset must eventually appear in all of its replicas. It must be possible to delete a junction, and to invalidate an FSN, in which case traversing a junction that refers to it must fail, and to invalidate an FSL, which must then never be returned as the result of resolving a junction.

R7 to R15 cover the namespace as a whole. The federation must be able to provide multiple namespaces, and it must be possible to query the file server named in an FSL to discover whether a junction exists at a given path, and possibly to list the junctions in that FSL. The projected namespace must be reachable by clients through at least one standard filesystem access protocol: CIFS, NFSv4, NFSv3 or NFSv2. It must be possible to modify the NSDB mapping to reflect the migration of a fileset from one FSL to another and the addition or removal of a replica, and both migration and replication should have little or no impact on clients, though the RFC notes that this depends on whether the source and destination servers can do it transparently, and that the administrator is responsible for recognising this. Objects should be annotatable with arbitrary name and value pairs for the use of higher-level protocols, such as recording the owner of an FSN. And it must be possible for the federation to project a namespace with a common root.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists the ground rules first, such as: clients should not need to know how the federation is arranged, the two sides must be able to authenticate each other, and the protocol must work with standard file sharing protocols. Then come fifteen requirements, covering naming, linking, moving files, and offering a shared top-level directory.

sections.title: What the Federation Need Not Do
sections.content:
Two things are listed as non-requirements.

N1. It is not necessary for the namespace to be known by any specific file server. In the same way that clients need no prior knowledge of the structure of the namespace or its mapping onto federation members, the projected namespace can exist without individual file servers knowing the whole organisational structure, or even exactly where in the projected namespace the filesets they host sit. File servers do need to handle referrals from other file servers, but they do not need to know what path the client was accessing when the referral was generated.

N2. It is not necessary for updates and accesses to the NSDB data to happen in a transaction or transaction-like context. The RFC explains that a requirement of this kind was considered and left out: the authors could not agree whether the benefits of transactions are worth the complexity they add, both to the specification and to its eventual implementation, and they say the topic is open for discussion. A draft of the proposed requirement is included, asking for a way to ensure that sequences of operations, including observations of the namespace and changes to it, can be performed with predictable semantics, and that sequences of operations can be protected by transactions with NSDB-wide or server-wide Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things are deliberately left out. No server has to know the whole picture, and the database of name-to-location mappings does not have to update atomically, because the authors could not agree that transactions were worth the complexity.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Assuming the Internet threat model, the federated resolution mechanism must be implemented so as to prevent loss of confidentiality, data integrity and peer entity authentication, as described in RFC 3552.

Confidentiality may be violated if an unauthorised party can eavesdrop on the communication between authorised servers and NSDB nodes and thereby learn the locations or other information about FSNs that they would not be authorised to discover by direct query. Data integrity may be compromised if a third party can undetectably alter the contents of that communication. Peer entity authentication is defeated if one server can masquerade as another without proper authority, or if an arbitrary host can masquerade as an NSDB node.

Well-established techniques for authenticated channels may be used to defeat these attacks, and the protocol must support at least one of them. If LDAP is used to implement the query mechanism, TLS can provide both authentication and integrity. If the query protocol runs on top of ONC/RPC, RPCSEC_GSS can fill the same role.

A federation could contain multiple PKI trust anchors, so the federation protocols should define a mechanism for managing a file server's NSDB trust anchors, and a general purpose trust anchor management protocol would be appropriate. The RFC also points out that the requirements lead naturally to a system with distributed authorisation, which has scalability and manageability benefits.

Because FSNs are likely to be long-lived resources, the privilege to create them should be carefully controlled. To help decide whether an FSN is referenced by a junction somewhere in the federation, the NSDB records should include non-authoritative informational annotations recording the locations of any such junctions. They are non-authoritative because a junction might be created, deleted or modified by someone who is not permitted to modify the NSDB records.
sections.plainLanguage: The lookups between servers and the name database must be protected, or an attacker could learn where files live, change the answers, or pretend to be the database. The document points at standard ways of doing that.

items.title: Fileset
items.text: The abstract view of a filesystem in the uniform namespace, backed by one or more physical filesystems.

items.title: FSN, fileset name
items.text: A platform-independent, globally unique name for a fileset. It survives migration and replication.

items.title: FSL, fileset location
items.text: Where a fileset is implemented at a particular moment, in a form the client can use.

items.title: Junction
items.text: A filesystem object linking a directory in one fileset to an object in another, by name rather than by location.

items.title: NSDB
items.text: The namespace database service that maps fileset names to their locations. It does not store junctions.

items.title: Referral
items.text: A server reply that sends the client to the same object at a different location, usually on another server.

items.title: Replica
items.text: A redundant implementation of a fileset. Each replica has the same name but a different location.
